name: Pechay
summary: How Filipino vegetable farmers usually grow pechay on beds, either sown in a seedbed and moved to the field or sown straight on the bed, up to the harvest about a month later. For backyard and small market growers who want the usual routine and what to change for more and cleaner leaves.
season: Pechay grows all year in the lowlands but does best in the dry, cooler months, roughly November to April. In the rainy months farmers plant on raised beds and under light cover, because heavy rain tears the leaves and brings rot. It grows from the lowlands up to mid elevations.
material: Seed, bought in small packs or cans. Farmers either sow it thinly in a seedbed or seedling tray and transplant the seedlings after two to three weeks, or broadcast or drill it straight on the bed and thin later.
spacing: Beds about 1 m wide with 20 to 25 cm paths. Plants 10 cm apart in rows 20 cm apart, one plant a hill. Direct sown beds are thinned to about the same.
water: Watered by hand every day with a watering can or hose in the morning or late afternoon, right after transplanting and until harvest. Larger fields are watered by furrow. Beds must drain well. Standing water rots the plants.
fertilizer: Traditional growers lean on chicken manure mixed into the beds, plus a little complete fertilizer (14 14 14) at planting and urea after one to two weeks. One common plot guide for a bed 1 m by 20 m is a sack of chicken manure, 1 kg of 14 14 14 and about 4 kg of urea worked into the soil before transplanting.
care: Daily watering, one or two hand weedings, thinning of direct sown beds, and close watch for leaf eating insects. Seedlings get a light shade and are hardened for a week before transplanting.
harvest: Pechay is ready three to four weeks after transplanting, or 30 to 40 days after direct sowing, while the leaves are tender. Farmers cut the plant at the base or pull it with the roots in the cool hours, wash it, remove yellow leaves, tie it in bundles and keep it shaded and moist.

ways.label: Seedbed then transplant (punla at lipat tanim)

steps.title: Plow and harrow
steps.how: Plow and harrow two or three times, about a week apart, to a depth of 15 to 20 cm so the soil is fine and the weeds are gone.

steps.title: Make the seedbed and sow
steps.how: Raise a seedbed about 1 m wide and 15 cm high with fine, clean soil. Sow the seed thinly in shallow lines or 2 to 3 seeds a hole in a seedling tray, cover lightly with fine soil and sprinkle with water.

parts.title: Build the bed
parts.how: Raise a bed about 1 m wide, 10 m long and 15 cm high in a sunny spot near water. Crush the clods and rake the soil until it is fine and loose.

parts.title: Clean the soil
parts.how: Spread dry rice straw over the bed and burn it, or pour boiling water over it and cover it with plastic until the soil cools. This kills the damping off fungus, weed seed and soil insects before sowing.

parts.title: Sow thinly in lines
parts.how: Water the bed first, then scratch shallow lines across it with a stick. Drop the seed thinly along the lines and cover it with a light sprinkle of fine soil.

parts.title: Or sow in a seedling tray
parts.how: Fill the tray holes with a clean potting mix and press it down lightly with the palm. Drop two or three seeds in each hole, cover them with fine soil and sprinkle with water.

parts.title: Keep it wet until they come up
parts.how: Sprinkle gently every morning or late afternoon so the top soil never dries out while the seed is sprouting. Use a can with a fine sprinkler head so the water does not wash the seed out.

steps.title: Shade and water the seedlings
steps.how: Give the young seedlings a simple roof against strong sun and hard rain, and water them in the morning or late afternoon.

steps.title: Prick out into small pots
steps.how: About five days after the seedlings come up, many growers move each one into its own small pot of rolled banana leaf, so it goes to the field with its roots in a ball of soil and does not wilt.

parts.title: Roll the banana leaf pots
parts.how: Cut banana leaf into strips, roll each strip into a small cup and fill it with the same clean soil mix used for the seedbed. Stand the pots close together in a box or on the bed.

parts.title: Lift the seedlings gently
parts.how: Loosen the seedbed soil with a small stick and lift the seedlings with a little soil on the roots. Hold them by a leaf, not by the thin stem, which bruises easily.

parts.title: One seedling a pot
parts.how: Make a hole in each pot with a finger, set one seedling in it and press the soil around it. Water the pots right away with a weak starter fertilizer mixed in water, or plain water.

parts.title: Shade them for a few days
parts.how: Keep the pots under the shed roof until the seedlings stand up again, then give them more sun each day until transplanting.

steps.title: Harden the seedlings
steps.how: Remove the cover bit by bit during the last week so the seedlings get used to full sun before they go to the field.

steps.title: Form the beds and put the base fertilizer
steps.how: Make beds about 1 m wide with paths of 20 to 25 cm between them. Mix chicken manure and a little complete fertilizer into the bed and cover it with soil.
steps.tip: Raise the beds higher in the rainy months so water runs off.

steps.title: Transplant in the afternoon
steps.how: Move seedlings that are two to three weeks old to the beds, 10 cm apart in rows 20 cm apart. Water right after planting.

steps.title: Water every day
steps.how: Water daily with a watering can or hose in the morning or late afternoon, enough to keep the bed moist but not soggy.

steps.title: Replace dead seedlings
steps.how: Fill any gaps with spare seedlings from the seedbed during the first week.

steps.title: Side dress and weed
steps.how: Many farmers give a little urea, often dissolved in water, along the rows about one to two weeks after transplanting, and pull the weeds at the same time.

steps.title: Check for pests twice a week
steps.how: Look under the leaves for aphids, small holes from flea beetles and the green larvae of the diamondback moth. Pull out and bury plants with soft, smelly rot or swollen roots.

steps.title: Wash, bundle and keep cool
steps.how: Wash off the soil, remove yellow leaves, tie in bundles and keep them in the shade, sprinkled with water, until they reach the market.

steps.title: Harvest in the cool hours
steps.how: Three to four weeks after transplanting, cut the plants at the base with a sharp knife or pull them with the roots, in the cool early morning or late afternoon.

watering.traditional: Pechay is watered by hand every day, with a watering can or a hose, in the early morning or late afternoon, from the seedbed until the day it is cut. Bigger lowland plots let water into the furrows between the beds instead, and the beds are kept raised so no water stands.
watering.method: A watering can with a fine head or a hose with a sprinkler nozzle, watering the soil and the base of the plants, is the usual way. Larger plots use furrows between the beds. Water in the early morning or late afternoon, never at noon, and early enough that the leaves dry before night.
watering.rainfed: Pechay is seldom grown on rain alone, because it needs water every day. Without a pump, plant near a well, a creek or a rain barrel and keep the plot small enough to water by can. Mulch the beds with rice straw or rice hull to keep the soil moist longer, and grow it in the rainy months under a simple cover.
watering.dryseason: In the dry months water every day, in the cool early morning or late afternoon, and a second time on very hot days if the plants droop. Water when the top soil feels dry to the touch. On sandy soil that is every day without fail.
watering.wet: Raise the beds higher and keep the paths open so rain runs off, and put a simple plastic roof over the beds if you can, because hard rain tears the leaves. Skip the watering on days the beds are already wet. Standing water rots the base of the plants and brings soft rot that smells bad.

schedule.often: Sprinkle the seedbed every morning or late afternoon so the top soil never dries
schedule.amount: A light sprinkle from a can with a fine head, just enough to darken the soil
schedule.why: The tiny seed sits near the surface and dies if the top soil dries even once, but a hard stream washes it out.

schedule.often: Water every morning or late afternoon
schedule.amount: Enough to moisten the bed or the pots, never soggy
schedule.why: Soil that stays wet in the shade brings damping off, which makes seedlings fall over at the base.

schedule.often: Water a little less often while the shade comes off. Water at once if the seedlings wilt hard
schedule.why: Seedlings used to full sun and less water stand the move to the field better.

schedule.often: Water the beds right after setting the seedlings in the afternoon
schedule.amount: Soak the soil around each plant
schedule.why: Water settles the soil around the roots so the plants stand up by the next morning.

schedule.often: Every day in the morning or late afternoon. Give a second light watering on very hot days if the plants still droop in the late afternoon
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the bed moist to the roots but not soggy. A 10 liter can covers a short stretch of bed, so walk it slowly
schedule.why: Pechay has short roots and grows fast only with steady moisture. Dry days make small, tough leaves.

schedule.often: Keep watering every day and harvest in the cool hours
schedule.why: Well watered plants are heavy and crisp and do not wilt on the way to market.

critical: The days the seed is sprouting: the top soil must never dry out.
The first days after transplanting, until the seedlings stand up again.
The whole leaf growth: pechay is harvested in about three weeks, so even two or three dry days show in the harvest.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and stay limp after the sun goes down, the leaves stay small and turn tough or bitter, and plants send up flower stalks early.
signs.wet: Lower leaves yellow, the base of the stem turns soft, brown and smelly, and seedlings fall over at the soil line.

better: Mulch the beds with rice straw or rice hull to keep the soil moist, cut the watering and stop rain from splashing soil on the leaves.
A drip line or a hose with a fine sprinkler gives even water to every plant and wastes less than splashing from a pail.

ways.label: Sown straight on the bed (sabog tanim)

steps.title: Prepare the beds
steps.how: Plow, harrow and form beds about 1 m wide, then rake manure or compost into the top soil.

steps.title: Sow the seed
steps.how: Broadcast the seed thinly over the bed, or drop it in shallow lines about 20 cm apart. Dust a little fine soil or rice hull over the seed and water gently.

steps.title: Keep the bed moist
steps.how: Sprinkle the bed every day until the seedlings are up, then water daily in the cool hours.

steps.title: Thin the seedlings
steps.how: Pull out extra plants so the rest stand about 10 cm apart. The thinnings can be cooked or sold.

steps.title: Side dress and weed
steps.how: Give a light side dressing of urea or manure tea and pull the weeds.

steps.title: Scout for leaf eaters
steps.how: Check the leaves for flea beetle holes, aphids and diamondback moth larvae, and remove rotting plants.

steps.title: Harvest the whole plant
steps.how: About 30 to 40 days after sowing, while the leaves are still tender, pull or cut the plants in the cool of the day.

watering.traditional: Seed sown straight on the bed is sprinkled every day until it comes up, then watered daily by can or hose in the cool hours until harvest. Larger plots are watered through the furrows between raised beds.
watering.method: A watering can with a fine head, or a hose with a sprinkler nozzle, is the usual way. Bigger plots water through the furrows between beds. Water in the early morning or late afternoon, never at noon.
watering.rainfed: Direct sown pechay needs water every day, so it is seldom left to rain alone. Without a pump, keep the bed close to a well or a rain barrel, cover the seed with rice hull, and mulch the bed with straw once the plants are up.
watering.dryseason: Water every day in the dry months, morning or late afternoon, and a second time on very hot days if the plants droop. Water whenever the top soil feels dry. Sandy beds need it daily without fail.
watering.wet: Sow on higher raised beds and keep the paths open so rain drains away. Hard rain can wash the seed out of a fresh bed, so a light cover of rice hull or a simple roof helps. Skip the watering on wet days. Standing water brings soft rot at the base.

schedule.often: Sprinkle the bed every day, morning or late afternoon, until the seedlings are up
schedule.amount: A light sprinkle from a can with a fine head, just enough to keep the top soil damp
schedule.why: The seed lies near the surface and dies if the top soil dries, while a hard stream washes it into clumps.

schedule.often: Water daily in the cool hours. Water before thinning so the extra plants pull out easily
schedule.amount: Enough to moisten the bed, never soggy
schedule.why: Young plants in a crowded bed rot at the base if the soil stays wet.

schedule.often: Every day in the morning or late afternoon. A second light watering on very hot days if the plants droop in the late afternoon
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the bed moist to the roots but not soggy
schedule.why: Steady moisture makes big, tender leaves. Dry days make small, tough ones and early flowers.

schedule.often: Keep watering daily and harvest in the cool of the day
schedule.why: Plants full of water are crisp and keep longer after cutting.

critical: Sowing to coming up: the top soil must stay damp every day.
The whole leaf growth: a few dry days make tough leaves and early flower stalks.

signs.dry: Seedlings come up patchy, leaves droop and stay limp after sundown, and the plants stay small, tough and send up flowers early.
signs.wet: Seedlings fall over at the soil line, lower leaves yellow, and the base of the plant goes soft and smells bad.

better: Cover the sown bed with rice hull and mulch the young plants with straw to keep the soil moist and cut the watering.
A fine sprinkler or drip line gives even water and keeps the seed from washing out.

mistakes: Sowing too thick and never thinning, so the plants come out thin and weak.
Watering at noon or letting water stand in the beds, which scorches leaves or brings soft rot.
Planting pechay right after cabbage, mustard or other cabbage family crops on the same bed again and again, so club root and diamondback moth build up.
Flat, low beds in the rainy months.
Harvesting at midday in the heat, so the leaves wilt before they reach the market.
better: Buy fresh seed of a variety suited to the season, with heat or rain tolerance for the wet months.
Test the soil and lime acid soils. Feed by the result with compost plus balanced fertilizer.
Use raised beds and a mulch of rice straw or plastic to keep the leaves clean and the weeds down.
Rotate pechay with crops outside the cabbage family, such as beans, corn or squash.
Scout twice a week and protect the seedbed with a fine net against leaf eating insects.
Harvest in the cool hours and keep the bundles shaded and moist on the way to market.
